 I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the

Commission, 19 Applicants hereby move for leave to submit this answer (“Answer”) to the

Protests. 20 As discussed herein, the Protests raise concerns that are meritless, unsupported,

irrelevant, and outside the scope of the Commission’s well-established merger analysis

framework under the FPA. This Answer explains why protesters’ arguments are without

merit and clarifies erroneous “facts” alleged by the protesters. The Commission regularly

accepts answers to protests where, as here, an answer promotes the Commission’s

understanding of the issues raised in the proceeding. 21 Good cause exists to accept this

Answer as it corrects misstatements of fact and law and will help the Commission make a

reasoned decision with respect to review of the Application.

II.       ANSWER

          A.      The Transaction Does Not Raise Market Power Concerns.

                1.      The Commission Should Adhere to its Precedents and Reject
                        Requests to Impose Different Tests.

        The Applicants performed Delivered Price Tests in accordance with 18 C.F.R.

§ 33.3 to analyze potential horizontal market power. The Commission has relied upon the

Delivered Price Test for nearly 30 years and has codified the test in its regulations. As the

Commission has explained, the test “[is] intended to identify mergers that clearly do not

raise competitive concerns early in the process and . . . produces a reliable, generally

conservative analysis of the competitive effects of a proposed merger.” 23 Despite the

Commission’s longstanding implementation and reliance on the Delivered Price Test,

certain protesters question whether the Delivered Price Test is the appropriate test to

measure horizontal market impacts. 24 The PJM IMM, for example, argues that the

Commission should instead apply the three pivotal supplier test. 25 The Commission has

repeatedly rejected the PJM IMM’s attempts to implement the three pivotal supplier test

         Statements from the State of Connecticut also undercut any argument that there is

a separate zero-carbon market. For there to be a separate, non-fungible relevant product,

the sellers of such product must have the ability to raise prices on such product, to a certain

extent, without decreasing demand for the product or buyers being able to meet their

demand by purchasing similar products elsewhere. Connecticut has certainly not paid a

premium for zero-carbon products; rather, the opposite is true. Governor Lamont’s

statement regarding this Transaction noted that “Connecticut’s nuclear contracts, which

provide energy at fixed prices and insulate ratepayers from volatile fossil fuel pricing have

saved Connecticut ratepayers more than $250 million in 2025 and $280 million so far in

2026 . . . .” 42 Moreover, recent requests for proposal (“RFPs”) issued by the State of

Connecticut have sought energy from nuclear, hydroelectric, new solar, and co-located

storage which are intended, in part, “to operate as a financial hedge against rising power

costs in the future.” 43 In other words, the RFPs are intended to save customers money

relative to what they might pay for fungible energy procured through the ISO-NE market,

not replace fossil-fuel energy with zero-carbon energy. The State Parties’ witness has also

acknowledged that zero-carbon resources compete against fossil fuel resources, stating in

           The Commission has previously declined to adopt such narrow product markets

within ISO-NE in its Section 203 analysis. For example, in NSTAR and Northeast

Utilities, 45 intervenors argued that procurement of wholesale electricity by utilities

competition in ISO-NE is between regulated utilities competing to supply POLR load”

acquired for state-regulated POLR service as a separate product market from otherwise

interchangeable wholesale electricity, the fact that Connecticut purchases electricity to

accomplish a legislatively specified zero-carbon objective does not transform those

purchases into a separate wholesale electricity product.

          The voluntary nature of the Connecticut procurements further undercuts the State

Parties’ argument.       Legislative or statutory authorization to procure resources is

substantially different from an inelastic legal obligation to acquire a fixed quantity of a

specific resource, irrespective of price. The purchasers in these procurements could simply

purchase through the ISO-NE markets rather than through the procurement if sellers

attempted to raise prices above competitive levels. The fact is that all generation resources

participating in the ISO-NE markets receive the same market price and all capacity

resources receive the same market price, regardless of their fuel source. Statements from

the State Parties’ witness, Connecticut’s Governor, and recent RFP announcements

acknowledge the competition among and between all generation resources in ISO-NE.

Therefore, the Commission should reject the attempt to introduce a Zero-Carbon

Generation as a separate wholesale electricity product in this proceeding.

                         b.      The Applicants Followed Well-Established Precedent in
                                 Allocating Capacity Subject to PPAs to the Purchaser.

than one year.” 49 Applicants have existing PPAs for portions of their nuclear capacity with

remaining commitments of more than one year (the “Millstone and Seabrook PPAs”). 50

Mr. Macan accordingly allocated the contracted capacity under those PPAs to the

purchasers. The State Parties assert that the Applicants should have assigned the contracted

         The Commission has long understood and explained that ownership does not

necessarily denote “control.” The Commission established its “guiding principle” for

determining control in Order No. 697, where it stated that “an entity controls the facilities

when it controls the decision-making over sales of electric energy, including discretion as

to how and when power generated by these facilities will be sold.” 52

         Contrary to the State Parties’ argument that the Applicants “retain control over

dispatch decisions for the Seabrook and Millstone plants,” 53 the Applicants do not retain

decision-making authority or discretion “as to how and when power generated by these

facilities will be sold” under the Millstone and Seabrook PPAs. 54
